text: Nonlinear mixing Nonlinear mixing Ray tracer datasets Home Ray-tracer Validation The orchard scenes The forest scenes Terms of use The authors Publications Data sets: orchards scenes One of the inputs of the ray-tracer is the geometry description of the different components. Geometry descriptions of two different vegetative systems were available to create data sets for the study of nonlinear mixing events: (i) citrus trees to recreate orchards, and (ii) poplar and beech trees to recreate mixed forest systems. The citrus trees are the trees as described in the ray-tracer and validation section. A total of ten trees were created by Stuckens et al. (2009), and calibrated based on ten trees in a commercial orchard in Wellinton, South Africa. These virtual trees encompass the large variability in tree structure (e.g. tree height, crown diameter, Leaf Area Index) encountered in the field. The Leaf Area Index, for example, ranged between 3.1 to 11. In the figure below, a virtual tree is shown next to the real tree in the orchard. Citrus leaf and stem optical properties are collected in the field using a field spectroradiometer and are used to calibrate the bidirectional scattering distribution functions. The soil background is simulated as a dry Luvisol, corresponding to the soil conditions in the study area. The total direct and diffuse irradiance as well as the angular distribution of diffuse irradiance is simulated with the SBDART atmospheric model at an angular resolution of 2Âº and subsequently implemented as the direct and hemispherical (diffuse) light sources in PBRT. A skymap is generated for a solar elevation and azimuth angle of 40.54Âº and 356.6Âº respectively, corresponding to the solar position at 10 August, 13 h local time in Wellington, South Africa. A virtual scene of a citrus orchard is recreated with one of the ten available tree structures in order to minimize the effects of endmember variability throughout the orchard. Replicas of this tree are placed in an orchard pattern. The orchard design is as such that it resembled the original orchard: an inter-row spacing of 4.5m, an inter-tree spacing of 2.5m, and a row azimuth of 7.3Âº. The soil background is uniform throughout the orchard. The spatial resolution is fixed at 2m to simulate hyperspectral airborne sensors. For the per-pixel reference data, both the spectral signatures of the soil and tree needs to be determined, and the areal coverage of these components within the pixel. Since the soil is uniform throughout the orchard, and only one tree is used to create the orchard, no variability in the endmembers is present, and one signature for each component can be used as a reference.  For the soil endmember, all trees are removed from the orchard, and the image is rendered again, providing the soil signature uncontaminated by the surrounding trees. For the tree endmember, the soil background of the orchard is replaced by a perfectly absorbing black background, to remove the influence of the background on the tree signature. A 5-cm resolution image of 4m by 4m was rendered above a canopy with one row (top figure on the right). Only the pixels containing a tree fraction greater than 0.95 were retained and averaged to provide the pure tree signature (bottom figure on the right). As such, the tree spectral signatures are an integration of all components of a tree, including sunlit and shaded leafs, branches, and stems. In addition, fraction maps are provided for the image, depicting the per-pixel tree- and soil fraction. Two different maps are provided: (i) the true areal coverage of the trees and the soil within the pixel, which sum up to one, and (ii) the sunlit areal coverage of each component, of which the sum will be smaller than one. The different datasets which are available will be posted below. For the moment, two orchard scenes are available, but more will follow. This results in only two-endmember mixtures. The scene consists of 20 by 20 pixels, with a spatial resolution of 2m. DOWNLOAD A citrus orchard with trees, weeds and soil present in the scene. This results in two- and three-endmember mixtures. The scene consists of 20 by 20 pixels, with a spatial resolution of 2m. To determine the weed endmember spectral signature, a similar approach to the tree endmember is used, replacing the soil background with a perfectly absorbing background, and removing all trees from the orchard. A 4m by 4m image with 1cm resolution is rendered over a weed patch, selecting only those pixels with a weed fraction greater than 0,95. These pixels are averaged to provide the spectral signature of the weeds. DOWNLOAD web development by Laurent Tits - aided by bryant smith
